source.title: DAVSP: Safety Alignment for Large Vision-Language Models via Deep Aligned Visual Safety Prompt
source.authors: Yi-Tong Zhang; Jia Li; Li-Yi Cai; Ge Li

record.file_problem: The full paper and appendices are present. Some tables are flattened in the supplied text, but their model, condition, and metric assignments are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The paper invokes shallow alignment as motivation for a new LVLM defense using activation-space supervision, but it does not test the claim’s fine-tuning, response-position KL, compliant-prefill, or weight-localization predictions.
record.gate_note: The study reports safety-defense results on harmful multimodal queries, including ablations and activation interventions. These test DAVSP and related defense behavior, not the specific claim versions; rows are therefore recorded as none and summarized under fits_no_version. The paper’s comparisons among defense methods and its utility results do not test the listed versions.
record.test_reason: The paper cites shallow alignment (Qi et al. 2024b) as motivation for DAVSP, a trainable visual padding prompt supervised in activation space for LVLMs. All reported results are the defense's own RSR and utility against baselines, its ablations, and activation interventions. It does not measure harmful or benign fine-tuning, per-token KL by response position, prefilling, weight localization, or how deep safety goes across response tokens. Its 'Deep Alignment' means activation-space supervision, not token depth, so it does not test V7 either. The one adjacent result is an adaptive image attack optimized for affirmative prefixes (Appendix I). It is a single sentence with an unclear baseline, and its purpose is to evaluate the defense. It is too thin to count as a V4 test.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that the visual safety prompt plus activation-space Deep Alignment resists malicious LVLM queries better than prior input-modification defenses with little utility loss, transfers across models, and needs both components. They also claim it addresses the shallow alignment of response-level training, but they do not measure token depth.
record.recipe_differences: The paper trains a visual input padding prompt for LVLMs using activation-space projection supervision and an auxiliary output loss; it does not use the original sources’ harmful/benign fine-tuning or per-token KL measurement recipes.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported sensitivity to padding size, supervision layer, and the loss balance coefficient λ. Larger padding generally raises resistance while gradually lowering benign utility; middle decoder layers give the best safety-utility trade-off; results remain stable across positive λ values in the tested range, while λ = 0 slightly reduces performance.

fits_no_version.finding: On two LVLMs, the DAVSP visual safety prompt plus activation-space supervision raises RSR over no defense and over baselines. Ablations show each component contributes, e.g. FigStep RSR 84.20 full, 67.00 without DA, 76.20 without VSP.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Activation-space supervision of an input-side visual prompt improves LVLM resistance to malicious multimodal queries more than output-level supervision alone.

fits_no_version.finding: Test-time shifts of the last-token hidden state along a harmful-minus-benign mean direction raise or lower RSR in the predicted direction.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A mean-difference harmfulness direction in mid-layer activations causally modulates LVLM refusal of malicious queries.

fits_no_version.finding: An adaptive image attack optimized for affirmative prefixes and low harmfulness projection gives FigStep RSR of 24% without DAVSP and 71% with it.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: DAVSP retains partial resistance to adaptive affirmative-prefix image optimization.

record.problems: Core experiments cover two LVLMs, with many ablations focused on LLaVA-1.5-13B; evaluation reports no error bars or confidence intervals. The main RSR assessment uses DeepSeek-V3 as an external judge; a human check sampled 130 responses and reports 96% agreement. The study does not directly evaluate the claim’s response-token depth or fine-tuning interventions.

untested.parts: No fine-tuning on harmful examples; model weights are frozen.
No per-token KL between aligned and base models.
No prefilling or decoding-change tests. The adaptive image attack targeting affirmative prefixes is reported only as one RSR figure with an unclear baseline.
No weight or rank localization. The harmfulness vector is an activation direction, not a parameter set.
The paper asserts that response-level objectives cause shallow alignment but tests no token-depth pattern.
The defense is called 'deep' but is never measured for safety across response positions or under prefill or fine-tuning attacks.

record.verdict_notes: The paper's 'shallow alignment' example (Figure 1: refusal, then harmful content) is illustrative only. Its choice of an LLM judge over keyword matching is motivated by shallow refusals, but it reports no rate of refuse-then-comply responses. Utility rows and the hyperparameter and ECSO integration results (Tables 1, 6, 8, 9; Appendix H) were reasonably left out because they bear on no version.

versions.untested_parts: No fine-tuning of a safety-trained chat model on harmful examples, and no few-to-hundreds-example compliance test.
No ordinary or carefully selected benign fine-tuning intervention measuring harmful compliance.
No per-token KL measurement between aligned and base models on harmful prompts.
No compliant-token prefilling, suffix, or decoding-change test. The adaptive attack optimizes images to encourage affirmative prefixes; it does not prefill one.
No localization or ablation of model weights or ranks carrying safety behavior; the trainable object is a visual input prompt.

The paper argues that response-level objectives can yield shallow alignment, but does not measure response-position shallowness or establish that data or objective causes the claimed token-depth pattern.
The paper trains activation-space supervision and measures safety rates, but does not measure whether safety is spread across response tokens or test token-depth robustness.
